prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: Reading the openings, I move my preferred configuration from circuit QED (my own first place) to optical lattice clocks. Four colleagues ranked B025 in their top four, two of them first, and the supporting arguments are independent of one another and unusually concrete. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the Doppler and recoil limits and allowed many atoms to be interrogated at once, and Ye's group drove the platform to about 10^-18 and into many-body clock physics. Independent national laboratories now reproduce and compare such clocks, so the result is robust. The two-name credit is clean and matches the supplied names exactly. The prize would reward a real regime change in measurement, and the work also enables tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The topic is far from the 2025 prize, which matters to me because that prize was awarded for macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is precision metrology and instrument development, so some will say it is an extraordinary technology rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon. The adjacent ground has been prized before (Hall and Hansch for the frequency comb in 2005, Wineland and Haroche in 2012), and the ion-clock community and groups such as SYRTE and PTB also made important contributions. I also have to admit that my own field is not B025, so my ranking of it rests on colleagues' judgement in AMO more than my own. If the committee wants a discovery-driven prize in the strict sense, B016 or B037 would be easier to justify, and B016 is my strongest scientific preference had the 2025 prize not just gone to circuits.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B025 first as a measurement capability that limits knowledge elsewhere, and in his B016 ballot he notes that the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes the timing sensitive and that Blais would be left out by a three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree with the precision argument for B025 and I think his timing point on B016 is fair and I underweighted it in my opening. Circuit QED was not what the 2025 prize recognised, but it is the same community and platform, and I am too close to it to judge how much distance the committee wants. I also agree with Kroll that a Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Girvin set (his proposal) and my Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Blais set are both defensible, so B016 would force a contested third name that B025 does not.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B025 first on the combination of Katori's idea and Ye's demonstrations, and flags the overlap with earlier metrology prizes, doubts about whether Ye's thorium nuclear-clock work belongs in a citation, and says B037 overlaps with Zoller's other candidacy.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the principal risk but I do not think it is decisive. The comb and ion-clock prizes recognised the enabling tools and single trapped ions, whereas the lattice clock is a distinct conceptual step with a different accuracy and stability regime. I would keep the citation to the lattice clock and leave the thorium nuclear clock out, since it is newer and not yet a mature result. Her concern about B037 is also fair, and it is one reason I place B037 only as an alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B025 seventh, asking whether the prize would be seen as technology and metrology rather than a physics discovery, and also asks about credit to the ion-clock community such as Wineland.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-technology concern seriously, and I disagree only in part. The lattice clock is built on a physical idea (magic-wavelength trapping that cancels the light shift) and its accuracy has opened tests of relativity at the millimetre scale and bounds on drifting constants, so the physics is part of the result. Where I agree with him is that the citation must emphasise this and not the engineering. Wineland's ion clocks were prized in 2012 for a different technique, so I see that as context and not a bar.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B025 second and notes its broad impact for geodesy and constants, while saying his atomic physics expertise is limited and he may lean on colleagues, and that Takamoto and Lemonde might be argued for.
responses.response: I appreciate that he is relying on AMO members, and I would add the same caution in reverse: I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on atomic-structure and clock details. On Takamoto and Lemonde, I think they were important contributors but the supplied names already identify the two people most clearly linked to the concept and to the record performance, and a three-person extension would dilute a clean attribution.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as a physics discovery or as metrology close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a prize to circuit QED should wait a few years after the 2025 prize, which I cannot judge objectively.
How much credit the early lattice-clock work (Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow) should receive relative to Katori and Ye; I have not verified the priority details independently.
Whether the B016 third laureate should be Blais or Girvin, if that candidate is later preferred.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue for B016 (circuit QED) and, to a lesser degree, B009: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, and have collaborated with experimental groups in this community, so I should not drive the decision on B016. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye (B025), or to B037 apparent from my profile.
